prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Restaurant Dinner Menu (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Starters" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Mains" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Desserts" spans 4 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Dish" · longest unbreakable word 77px · one-line width 164px
  col 2: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 558px
  col 3: header "Price" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 37px
  col 4: header "Allergens" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 298px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Help diners choose dishes by comparing their descriptions, prices and allergens within each course.","reading":"Readers scan course headings and dish names first, then read across a row for details; the course headings span the full table and should remain distinct from dish rows.","groups":["Dish and Description belong together as the name and explanation of each menu item.","Price and Allergens are compact decision aids that readers compare across dishes."],"keep_intact":["Price values and the Price header","Individual words in dish names, descriptions and allergen lists","The association between each dish and its price and allergens"],"may_wrap":["Descriptions can wrap naturally at word spaces.","Multiword dish names can wrap when needed.","Allergen lists can wrap at natural breaks; description wrapping may already provide enough row height to accommodate them."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r0A: widths [185, 340, 58, 136] · table 720×467px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 60, 36, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0B: widths [150, 310, 58, 201] · table 720×490px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 83, 36, 83, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0C: widths [120, 400, 58, 141] · table 720×490px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 83, 36, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
